deep.reconstruction:
The page has no text, formulas or numbers apart from the library stamp. It holds a single carefully ruled diagram in black/brown ink, thick grey-brown wash lines and thin red lines, with faint pencil underdrawing: a short pencil baseline at the bottom, a faint horizontal pencil line about one third of the way down, and small pencil marks near the bottom points.

What is drawn:
(a) A convex lens, shown as a thin biconvex lens-shaped outline, sits about two thirds of the way down, with its axis vertical.
(b) Bundle 1 (black/dark brown) is three vertical lines parallel to the axis. They meet the lens at its left rim, centre and right rim. Below the lens the two rim rays become thin dark lines that converge, with the central undeviated ray, to a single point on the axis at the baseline. This is the paraxial focus F.
(c) Bundle 2 (thick brown/grey wash) is three parallel oblique lines coming from the upper right and descending to the left. They strike the left rim, centre and right rim. Below the lens they converge to one point on the baseline to the left of F. The middle line of this bundle crosses the lens centre undeviated and is the chief ray.
(d) Bundle 3 (thin red) is three parallel oblique lines coming from the upper left. Below the lens they converge to one point on the baseline to the right of F (lower right corner of the figure).
(e) All three convergence points lie on the same horizontal pencil baseline.

Interpretation (mine): this is a didactic or working sketch of image formation of objects at infinity by a converging lens. Each parallel bundle of field angle theta is brought to a focus at the point where its undeviated chief ray meets the focal plane. In modern notation, for a thin lens of focal length f, a ray of height h and slope tan(theta) leaves the lens with slope tan(theta) - h/f. At distance f it reaches x = h + f*tan(theta) - h = f*tan(theta), independent of h. So all rays of the bundle meet at x = f*tan(theta) on a flat focal plane, as drawn.

Context: the next leaf (7r) contains Gauss's 'formula approximata' versus 'formula exacta'. These are paraxial versus exact trigonometric ray tracing through spherical refracting surfaces (sin A = (a-r) sin(phi)/r, sin B = sin A / n, phi' = phi + A - B, a' = r + r sin B / sin phi' - h), with numerical lens data, apparently around 1841. The present sketch very likely visualises the paraxial picture whose accuracy those computations test. It shows the ideal (aberration-free, flat-field) focusing of on-axis and off-axis parallel pencils by an objective. No quantitative content can be extracted.
errors: No computational errors are possible, since there is no text. The drawing is idealised: all rays of each oblique bundle meet exactly in one point on a flat focal plane. This ignores spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism and field curvature, which the exact formulas on the next page are designed to quantify. It is a schematic, not a mistake.
The rim rays of the oblique bundles are drawn somewhat freehand (wash lines of uneven width), so the convergence is only approximately exact in the drawing.

results.what: Diagram: parallel pencils at different field angles focused by a convex lens to points on a common (flat) focal plane, located where the undeviated chief ray through the lens centre meets that plane
results.modern_name: Paraxial (Gaussian) imaging of objects at infinity; focal plane, image height y' = f tan(theta); chief ray through optical centre
results.usually_credited_to: Classical geometrical optics (Kepler, Huygens, Newton, 17th century); systematised paraxially by Gauss, Dioptrische Untersuchungen (1841)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a textbook-level ray diagram of focusing of parallel bundles by a lens, with no formulas. It is entirely routine, and Gauss's work on paraxial dioptrics (1841) is well known.

checkable.sympy: h, f, t = symbols('h f t'); simplify((h + f*(t - h/f)) - f*t) == 0
checkable.asserts: Thin lens: a ray of height h and slope t = tan(theta) reaches the focal plane at x = f*t, independent of h. So every parallel bundle focuses at one point on the focal plane, as drawn.

checkable.sympy: h, f = symbols('h f'); simplify(h + f*(0 - h/f)) == 0
checkable.asserts: Axis-parallel rays (theta = 0) all meet the axis at the focal point, which is the central convergence point of the black bundle.

transcription_corrections: The page contains no handwritten text. Besides the stamp there is a faint horizontal pencil line in the upper third, a short pencil baseline at the bottom joining the three focal points, and small pencil scribbles near the bottom convergence points. These are not reflected in the transcription.
The lens is drawn as a thin biconvex (lens-shaped) outline rather than a true ellipse, with pointed ends at the rims where the rays meet.
